rv.q: When Walker gnaws a fingernail, it seems as though she might devour an entire finger without noticing.

Payne’s new play needs a bit of time to show itself, but Walker’s molten performance grabs you instantly – together they paint a haunting but disarmingly funny portrait of grief turning into something else, that elicits a career best performance from its star.
Now she triumphs again in Nick Payne's new play, with an extraordinary evocation of entrenched sorrow and feral anxiety.
What does hold the play back is that the framing of characters’ attempts to grapple with the inexplicable sometimes feels too strategic and rather obvious: a séance, a discussion of religious faith.
For Walker fans, the play is a must. But this undeniably brave piece left me feeling oddly uninvolved.
This is a sincere, empathetic and surprisingly funny work from the award-winning writer of Constellations and We Live In Time, but it’s also relentless and lacking in tonal variety.
In a way, despite the careful construction of ideas and oppositions, it ultimately feels as though Payne’s play is equally frustrated in its attempt to grasp at substance.
But while her star turn has rightly ensured a sell-out run for Marianne Elliott’s assured production, it’s not enough to convert the sceptical to the play itself.
The Unbelievers may divide people as a result: is it hypnotic and affecting, as I found it, or merely monotonous?
It's always a bad sign, however, when you catch yourself admiring the actors' technique rather than caring about the characters they represent.
This is unquestionably dramatic subject matter with resonances to so many news stories on disappeared children, but it just does not cut deeply enough.
I am so glad to have experienced it – a play to remember for a long time, especially the next time I read or hear of someone who is ‘missing’ or ‘disappeared’.
Walker’s performance takes no prisoners, thoroughly unconcerned with the opinion of others.
I, for one, believe in the gathering power with which The Unbelievers argues its unflinching case, and Walker's complete embrace of this role is itself a thing of wonder.
Flawed as it sometimes is, The Unbelievers is a fine piece of work gifted with a stunning central performance.
Ultimately this gripping family drama taps into the zeitgeist for negotiating private grief in a loud and accelerating world.
Though the play is uneven as a whole, in the central role of Miriam, Nicola Walker delivers an astonishing, raw portrayal of a mother navigating a terrible sea of complex emotions.
The tonal inconsistencies may be deliberate, but they make for a frustrating experience overall.
One of Payne's finest plays though, The Unbelievers confirms the Royal Court's new phase can again splice the traditionally-crafted with the exploratory. A must-see.
The Unbelievers lives up to expectations; insightful, humane, dramatic and surprisingly funny, this story of a missing child is so admirably crafted, it has it all.

Walker is pitch-perfect as a mother at the end of her wits, her insurmountable grief isolating her from her family, while the terrific supporting cast deliver equally layered, compelling performances.
The decision to have actors who are not needed for a particular scene wait upstage in a waiting room is a simple but genius way of reinforcing the show’s themes.

Nicola Walker is tremendous as Miriam, capturing both her passionate determination to find her missing son and the destructive effect it has on the rest of the family, in a rounded portrayal of abrasive provocation, emotional fragility, and barbed humour.

The Unbelievers is a slightly frustrating watch. There are moments of powerful and raw emotion from an excellent cast. But, despite an attempt to mask it with the jumping timeline, the story doesn't really go anywhere.
There's something about The Unbelievers that didn't quite connect with me, some detachment that I couldn't quite find a way past.

cn.t: Walker delivers a powerhouse performance in Payne's time-fractured drama about a mother unable to move on from her missing son, but critics find the play uneven—praised for its emotional intensity and dark humor yet criticized for lacking the elegance of his earlier work.
